verses.translation_literal: A Maskil of David, in his being in the cave, a prayer.
verses.translation_dramatic: A song of insight, David's own, set down from the day he was in the cave. A prayer.
verses.directors_commentary:
This line is the title the first singers heard before the music began, and it tells the actors where to stand: inside rock, in the dark, with a door of light behind them. The Hebrew says only "the cave", with the article, as if everyone knew which one. Tradition fills it in: Rashi names the cave of 1 Samuel 24, where David cut the corner of Saul's robe; Radak and Meiri say the same, though 1 Samuel 22 (Adullam) is also possible. A cave in the Judean hills was a refuge and a trap at once, one mouth and no back door.

The KJV prints this as "Maschil of David; A Prayer when he was in the cave" and numbers it as verse 0, so its verse 1 is our verse 2. "Maschil" is left untranslated: it is a term of the singers, probably a skilled or instructive song (Ibn Ezra hears "a sweetness of poetry"). Note the word order: "prayer" comes last, so that the word hangs in the air as the title closes.

philological_notes.note: A heading term of uncertain meaning, from the root 'to have insight, to act wisely'. It may mark a skilled, reflective or instructive composition. It is left transliterated in the KJV.
'In the cave', with the article: a known cave. Rashi links it with the cave where David cut Saul's robe.

verses.translation_literal: My voice, to YHWH, I cry out; my voice, to YHWH, I seek favor.
verses.translation_dramatic: My voice goes to the LORD, and I cry. My voice goes to the LORD, and I beg for grace.
verses.directors_commentary:
The first line is two short blows with the same shape: "my voice to YHWH", twice, with a different verb each time. "I cry out" (אזעק) is the shout of someone wronged, the word used for the oppressed calling for a rescuer. "I seek favor" (אתחנן) comes from חנן, grace: it is the speech of a person with no claim, asking for a gift. The first verb is loud, the second pleading, and the actor can let the volume drop on the repeat.

Hebrew has no verb in the phrase "my voice to YHWH"; it is a clipped, nearly breathless opening, and Meiri says a "with" is missing: "with my voice I cry to YHWH". The KJV adds "I cried" in the past and "with my voice" as an instrument, which smooths the clipped fragment into a calm sentence, and puts both verbs in the past tense though the Hebrew verbs are present. Malbim adds a stage direction: in a cave full of fugitives and with enemies nearby, a loud voice is dangerous. To YHWH alone he can raise it without fear.

philological_notes.note: Hithpael of חנן: 'to make oneself the object of grace', that is, to plead for favor. It is the speech of the one who has no claim.
'My voice', repeated for emphasis; Meiri reads a missing 'with' (בקולי). Malbim hears the cave: he dares to raise his voice only to God.

verses.translation_literal: I pour out before him my complaint; my trouble before him I tell.
verses.translation_dramatic: I pour it out before him, all my murmuring and grief. Before him I lay out my trouble, and I tell it, to the end.
verses.directors_commentary:
The center of this verse is the picture of water poured from a jar: "I pour out" (אשפך). Nothing is held back and the vessel is emptied; the same verb is used for blood and for a heart poured out in Psalm 62:9 and in Hannah's prayer. "Before him" (לפניו) is placed at the front of both lines, and it is the only fixed point: the person pours, and the speaker's face is toward God. The KJV's "complaint" is fair, but shaded toward a grumbling that "שיח" does not have; the word is closer to a murmured musing, a talk to oneself, and Metzudat Zion defines it as telling troubles.

The second verb "I tell" (אגיד) is a courtroom-like verb: to declare a matter in front of someone. Radak adds that God knows already, and the poet tells him anyway. Malbim splits the two lines in an interesting way: the poured-out complaint is the inward grief, and the told trouble is the outward danger. In a dark cave nobody else can be told.

philological_notes.note: 'My complaint, my musing': speech that is half-muttered, half-meditated. Not an accusation, though KJV's 'complaint' can sound like one. Radak glosses it simply as 'my prayer'; Metzudat Zion as the telling of troubles.
'I pour out', the verb for liquid, and for blood. Meiri says the pouring is a figure for the abundance of the prayer.

verses.translation_literal: In the wrapping over me of my spirit, and you, you know my pathway; in the path which I walk they have hidden a snare for me.
verses.translation_dramatic: My spirit folds in on itself, wrapped over me like a cloak, and I am faint. But you, you know my path. On the very road I walk, they have hidden a snare for me.
verses.directors_commentary:
The verse has three beats. First comes the collapse: "my spirit wraps itself over me" (בהתעטף עלי רוחי), the verb used for fainting in Psalm 102:1 and for a person bent over and folded in on himself. Radak says the body curls in on itself, with the spirit inside it. Then the pivot: "and you" (ואתה), a short and hard contrast. Everyone else is blind, and God alone knows the path. Rashi hears a darker note under the word "path": God knows how many traps are laid along it.

Then the cause of the fainting arrives: "they have hidden a snare" (טמנו פח). The word פח is a fowler's trap or net, set in the open on the path where a bird will walk, and the verb "hide" means to bury it under dust or leaves. The KJV's "privily laid a snare" is both archaic and a little abstract, and it turns a hunter's image into a general plot. Note too that the KJV's "then thou knewest" invents a "then", as if the knowing followed the fainting; the Hebrew simply sets the two side by side. A listener in the ancient world knew the sight of a snare in a path: the hunted man is the bird.

philological_notes.note: Hithpael infinitive: 'in the wrapping itself over', i.e. fainting, collapse. The same root is used in Psalm 102:1 for the afflicted who 'faints'. Radak compares Psalm 107:5, 'their soul faints within them' (נפשם בהם תתעטף); the image is one of folding in on oneself.
A bird-trap or snare, a net or noose set in the open and covered. The image of the hunter and the bird recurs through the Psalms.

verses.translation_literal: Look at the right hand and see, and there is none for me who acknowledges; refuge is lost from me; there is none who seeks for my soul.
verses.translation_dramatic: Look to the right and see: there is no one there who knows me. Every place of flight has vanished from under me. No one asks after my life.
verses.directors_commentary:
In the ancient world the right side was the place of the defender. A witness or advocate stood at the right hand of the accused, as in Psalm 109:31 and 121:5. So "look to the right" asks where the helper is, and the answer is an empty space. Radak and Meiri note that the "right" stands for all sides, as the text speaks briefly. The first two verbs are imperatives, and they are addressed to God: "look, and see." Radak and Ibn Ezra take them as infinitives ("I looked ... and saw"), as the KJV does, which turns the plea into a narrative.

Three losses follow, each in a short hard clause. "There is none who acknowledges me" (אין לי מכיר): the word means to recognize someone as one of yours, and the legal sense is of the kinsman who stands up and says "this man is mine". "Refuge is lost" (אבד מנוס): the place to flee to has perished. "No one seeks for my soul" (אין דורש לנפשי): the verb "seek" (דרש) also means to inquire after or to avenge; the same verb is used of the avenger of blood in Psalm 9:13. The KJV's "no man cared for my soul" makes it a matter of sentiment, whereas the Hebrew is closer to "no one asks after my life, no one will claim it". Radak says it plainly: against a king's hand, no kinsman redeemer will come.

philological_notes.note: 'One who recognizes, acknowledges': the Hiphil participle of נכר. To 'recognize' someone is to claim them as one's own. KJV 'know me' loses the legal-social sense.
'One who seeks, inquires after, cares for'. It is also used for a person who 'requires' a life as an avenger. Radak ties it to the lack of a redeemer.
A place of flight, a refuge to run to. Radak says: wherever he goes, Saul seeks him.

verses.translation_literal: I cry out to you, YHWH; I say, You are my refuge, my portion in the land of the living.
verses.translation_dramatic: So I cry out to you, O LORD. I say it: you are my refuge. You are my portion in the land of the living.
verses.directors_commentary:
After three verses of what others have failed to do, the speaker turns to the one who remains. The verb "I cry out" returns from verse 2, and this time it has a direct address: "to you", no longer "to him". The speaker has moved from talking about God to talking to God. The shift of person is the turning point of the poem, and the actor should let the voice change.

The key words are "refuge" and "portion". "Refuge" (מחסי) is the shelter of a bird under wings or a man in a rock, set in contrast to the lost "place of flight" (מנוס) of the verse before: human refuge is lost, but YHWH is a refuge. "Portion" (חלקי) is a word of land and inheritance: each tribe received a "portion", and the Levites were told YHWH was theirs (Num 18:20). To say "you are my portion" is to say that God is the plot of ground on which he stands, in a hole in the ground with nothing. The KJV's "thou art my refuge and my portion" adds "and" which the Hebrew leaves out; it is two bare statements side by side. "The land of the living" is the world of the living as against Sheol, where the dead are not (Ps 27:13). Radak reads this as the land of Israel, which he is fleeing; Meiri also allows the world to come; Metzudat David reads it simply: I will not die at Saul's hand.

philological_notes.note: 'My portion', an allotment of land or inheritance. Radak connects it with 'YHWH is the portion of my inheritance and my cup' (Ps 16:5).

'The land of the living': the world of the living, in contrast to Sheol. Radak reads it as the land of Israel; Meiri as this world or the world to come; Metzudat David as life here, not death at Saul's hand.

verses.translation_literal: Give heed to my cry, for I have become very low; rescue me from those who pursue me, for they are stronger than I.
verses.translation_dramatic: Listen to my cry, for I have fallen very low. Pull me out of the hands of those who hunt me, for they are stronger than I am.
verses.directors_commentary:
Two petitions, each with its reason, in the pattern of a plea before a judge: "Listen, for..." and "Rescue me, for...". The word for cry here is a new one, רנה, which usually means a ringing shout of joy and is used here for a shout of distress; Radak compares it with 1 Kings 22:36, a shout passing through the camp. It is a high-pitched, carrying sound, not the muttering of verse 3, and in a cave it would be the dangerous kind.

"I have become very low" (דלותי מאד) comes from דלל, to hang low, to be thin and weak. The related noun דל is the poor and weak man, and Metzudat David glosses the verb in just those terms: "I have become poor and subdued". The speaker, once a warrior at court, now counts himself among the weak. The KJV's "brought very low" makes the lowness something done to him; the Hebrew is simply "I have become low". "Those who pursue me" is a participle, "my pursuers" (רדפי), and it is the military word for a chase; for David, Saul's army. The KJV's "persecutors" takes it into the language of religious persecution and misses the hunt. Radak states the reason: he cannot stand against a king and his people. The last clause, "they are stronger than I" (אמצו ממני), uses the same root as the command "be strong" (חזק ואמץ) in the war narratives of Joshua.

philological_notes.note: 'My ringing cry'. Usually a shout of joy, here a shout of need. Radak glosses it as 'my cry', citing the shout that passed through the camp.
'I have become low, weak'. Related to the noun דל, the poor and weak man. Metzudat David: 'I have become poor and subdued.'
'They are stronger', 'they have become mighty'. Metzudat Zion: חזקו.

verses.translation_literal: Bring out from the prison my soul, to give thanks to your name; around me the righteous will gather as a crown, for you will deal fully with me.
verses.translation_dramatic: Bring my soul out of its prison, that I may give thanks to your name. The righteous will gather around me, a crown, when you deal bountifully with me.
verses.directors_commentary:
The prayer ends where it began, in the cave. "Prison" (מסגר) is a word for a lock or a confinement; it is a cave, as Radak says, in which he was shut in. The KJV's "prison" is correct, but it is the word that makes the cave a place of stone and bars. The speaker's own soul (נפש), in the Hebrew, is what is imprisoned, so that the plea is for his whole self, not only for his body. The reason he gives is not comfort but thanks: "to give thanks to your name". Meiri hears in it: he wants to be free, to give thanks. The Hebrew "to give thanks" (להודות) is also "to confess, to acknowledge publicly", so the vow is of a public thanksgiving in front of others.

The next clause is the most disputed. "Bi yakhtiru tzaddiqim" (בי יכתרו צדיקים): the verb is from כתר, and the noun is כתר, a crown or circlet. Rashi and Radak read it as a crown: the righteous will make me their crown, or will crown God because of me; Ibn Ezra reads the sense as boasting, as with a royal crown on the head. The KJV's "compass me about" is the reading of a circle of people who gather around him, a reading that fits the root's sense of "to surround" and appears in Judges 20:43. The Hebrew allows both: a crowd that ring him round like a crown. The final "for you will deal fully with me" (כי תגמל עלי) means to repay, to complete a measure; here it is for good, as in Psalm 13:6. The KJV and ASV are close to it.

philological_notes.note: 'A place of closing, a confinement': a prison, or here the cave in which he is shut. Radak: because he was shut in the cave. Malbim hears a spiritual image: the soul is shut in the cave and cannot serve God.
From כתר 'to surround', related to כתר 'crown'. The sense is disputed: 'gather around me' (KJV), 'make a crown of me' (Radak) or 'crown you because of me' (Rashi).
'You will deal fully, requite'. The root is neutral; here the context makes it a favor.
